key_insight: LLMs that exhibit fewer measurable cognitive biases do not always make better decisions; some biases can be functional and improve context-specific outcomes. Reducing bias indiscriminately can therefore degrade decision quality in certain tasks.
problem_solved: Challenges the assumption that lowering cognitive bias in LLMs universally improves decision-making, and clarifies the relationship between bias metrics and real-world decision performance.
method: Systematic evaluation of cognitive-bias metrics across multiple LLMs and decision-making tasks to compare bias levels with decision outcomes.
Task-based analyses that measure contextual performance (accuracy, utility, or task-specific success) alongside standard bias assessments.
Comparative interpretation showing when bias correlates positively, negatively, or neutrally with decision quality, emphasizing context-dependent effects.
impact: Prompts AI practitioners to move beyond one-size-fits-all debiasing: evaluate biases in the context of downstream task utility and design targeted interventions that preserve beneficial, adaptive heuristics while mitigating harmful ones.
visual_elements: Scatter plot: bias metric (x-axis) vs decision quality (y-axis) showing non-monotonic relationship and clusters where lower bias does not mean better outcomes.
Flowchart of the evaluation pipeline: bias measurement → decision task → performance comparison → contextual interpretation.
Side-by-side examples: model outputs before/after debiasing with task-specific success indicators (checkmark/x and short explanations).
Icon set: 'Bias' (brain with bias), 'Decision' (scales), and 'Context' (target) to illustrate that effectiveness depends on task context.
paper_title: LLMs displaying less cognitive bias are not necessarily better decision makers
paper_authors: Vittoria Dentella, Marco Marelli, Luca Rinaldi
